title: How to give feedback that changes behaviour, not just feelings

audience.knows: Everyday workplace conversations; no formal feedback framework assumed
audience.cares_about: Making feedback useful without turning a working relationship into a personal judgement

outcome: Rewrite feedback they need to give so the colleague can identify the behaviour to change and the next action to try.
through_line: Make an actionable change, rather than a judgement of the person, the destination of the feedback.

arc_plan.what: Establish an explicitly hypothetical workplace feedback dilemma: the recipient has a reaction, but still needs to know what to do differently.
Set the practical destination: the viewer will revise feedback they need to give into guidance a colleague can act on.
Use the same dilemma to distinguish the desired workplace behaviour from the emotional response to the conversation, without treating feelings as irrelevant.
Develop an approved method for turning feedback about workplace behaviour into a clear next action. Use the running example to reveal each part before naming it.
arc_plan.needs: An approved knowledge sheet establishing the feedback method, its rationale and its limits; the requester supplied a topic, not a method.

arc_plan.what: Have the viewer distinguish actionable feedback from feedback that merely sounds considerate, using revisions of the running example and the approved method's criteria.
arc_plan.needs: Verified criteria for judging the revisions and explaining the correct choice.

arc_plan.what: Invite the viewer to adapt the verified method to feedback they actually need to give, identifying the behaviour and the next action they want to discuss.
arc_plan.needs: The approved method and any context limits needed for safe workplace application.

arc_plan.what: Return to the opening dilemma with the feedback revised and the intended next action made clear. Resolve the communication problem without depicting guaranteed behaviour change.
arc_plan.needs: A resolution consistent with the approved method and its limits.

must_cover.what: The requester's distinction between feedback aimed at changing behaviour and feedback that only affects feelings.
An evidence-backed, usable method for making feedback about workplace behaviour actionable.
The distinction between describing behaviour and judging the person, if supported by the approved knowledge sheet.
A genuine practice check that tests whether the recipient can identify what to do differently, with criteria grounded in the approved method.
Transfer to the viewer's own workplace feedback, including the method's relevant limits rather than a promise of compliance.

must_avoid: Opening with abstract terminology or an agenda
A survey of feedback frameworks instead of a usable method
Disconnected examples that do not return to the central dilemma
Trivia checks or choices based only on politeness
Unsupported statistics, learning-styles claims or invented quotations presented as real
Presenting hypothetical dialogue or outcomes as a real workplace account
Treating feelings as irrelevant or useful feedback as permission to be harsh
Promising that wording alone will make another person change
A superior, schoolroom or childish tone
example_posture: Use an explicitly hypothetical, ordinary workplace feedback dilemma as the running example. Keep the behaviour and its requested change concrete, but select the situation only after the approved method is available. Revisit the same dilemma for the explanation, practice check and resolution. Do not invent a real colleague, testimonial or successful result.
visual_direction: Honour the requested story-cartoon style with a restrained illustrated workplace situation and a visible contrast between unclear feedback and a recognisable next action. Let the same situation evolve rather than replacing it with unrelated pictures. Keep the classic flat illustration approach available; a more dimensional or performed treatment can be offered as an alternative, not substituted silently. Use an adult visual tone and legible captions. Character acting has not been selected.
voice_note: Use the requested mentor persona as a capable colleague helping someone prepare a difficult conversation. Be warm, direct and practical, without moralising or implying that the viewer has been doing feedback wrong.
open_questions: No approved knowledge sheet was supplied, and no factual claims or feedback method have been verified. Establish the method, rationale, assessment criteria and limits before filling the flagged segments.
Is the intended context peer-to-peer feedback, manager-to-employee feedback or both? The brief provisionally uses a general colleague relationship.

The requester specified story-cartoon and a woman presenter, but did not choose plain versus cinematic storytelling or illustrated faces versus character acting. Preserve that uncertainty rather than treating the presenter choice as permission for acting.
